title: Bài sưu tầm 229 - Passage 2: Reclaiming the Salt Marsh: Coastal Defence Without Concrete
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 229

Reclaiming the Salt Marsh: Coastal Defence Without Concrete

Paragraph 1. For generations, the standard response to rising tides along populated coastlines was to build taller concrete seawalls. Yet coastal engineers increasingly recognize that rigid barriers carry a hidden structural flaw. When powerful storm waves slam into a vertical wall, the reflected energy plunges straight downward, scouring away the protective layer of sand in front of the barrier. Over time, this erosion undermines the wall's foundations, leading to sudden collapse unless crews repeatedly dump expensive rock armour along the base.

Paragraph 2. An alternative approach, known as 'managed realignment,' is transforming low-lying shores in eastern England. At Wallasea Island in Essex, engineers deliberately opened gaps in aging earthen embankments to invite tidal seawater back onto former grazing fields. To raise the sunken land up to tidal level, barges delivered three million tonnes of clay excavated during the construction of a major underground railway beneath London. Within months of flooding, pioneer salt-tolerant plants began colonising the wet mudflats.

Paragraph 3. Unlike concrete, a living salt marsh absorbs wave energy gently rather than fighting it head-on. Dense clusters of flexible cordgrass bend beneath incoming surges, reducing wave height by as much as sixty percent across the first forty metres of vegetation. Equally valuable is the marsh's capacity to adapt to changing conditions. Tangled networks of roots trap fine silt carried inland by high tides, allowing the marsh floor to rise gradually alongside climbing sea levels without requiring heavy machinery.

Paragraph 4. Monitoring at Wallasea soon revealed an unexpected climatic bonus. Because tidal mud remains waterlogged throughout the year, it contains virtually no oxygen, which slows microbial decay dramatically. Dead plant stems sink into the mud and remain locked underground for centuries rather than releasing carbon dioxide back into the sky. Measured per hectare, healthy coastal marshes store carbon several times faster than mature inland woodlands.

Paragraph 5. Despite these ecological gains, breaching old flood banks often triggers local friction. Neighbouring arable farmers initially worried that advancing seawater might seep underground and contaminate freshwater wells used for irrigation. To resolve these concerns, planners constructed secondary drainage ditches along the inland perimeter and compensated landowners for flooded pasture.

Paragraph 6. Five years after the embankments were opened, biological surveys confirmed a broader economic payoff. Sheltered creeks winding through the restored marsh quickly filled with juvenile sea bass and other commercial fish, using the shallow reeds as a nursery safe from deep-water predators. For coastal planners, the lesson is clear: working with tidal rhythms can deliver flood safety, carbon storage, and thriving fisheries at a fraction of concrete maintenance costs.

q14.text: Vertical concrete seawalls help keep protective beach sand in place during heavy storms.

steps: Đoạn 1: Sóng đập vào tường bê tông dội ngược xuống dưới, cuốn trôi lớp cát bảo vệ phía trước (scouring away the protective layer of sand).

q15.text: Transporting London tunnel clay to Wallasea Island by barge cost less than transporting it by road.

steps: Đoạn 2: Có nhắc đến việc dùng sà lan (barges) chở đất sét đào từ đường hầm London tới Wallasea, nhưng hoàn toàn không so sánh chi phí giữa đường thủy và đường bộ.

q16.text: Salt marshes are able to adjust their elevation naturally without mechanical assistance.

steps: Đoạn 3: "allowing the marsh floor to rise gradually alongside climbing sea levels without requiring heavy machinery."

q17.text: Dead marsh plants decompose rapidly in waterlogged mud, releasing carbon into the air.

steps: Đoạn 4: Bùn ngập nước thiếu oxy làm quá trình phân hủy chậm lại đáng kể, giữ carbon hàng thế kỷ thay vì thải lên trời.

q18.text: Restoring tidal wetlands at Wallasea Island yielded commercial fishery benefits within five years.

steps: Đoạn 6: Sau 5 năm mở đê, khảo sát cho thấy các lạch cạn đầy cá vược con và các loài cá thương mại.
Đoạn 3: "reducing wave height by as much as sixty percent" (sixty percent ↔ over half).
Đoạn 3: "Tangled networks of roots trap fine silt" (tangled networks ↔ interwoven; silt ↔ mud).
Đoạn 4: "contains virtually no oxygen, which slows microbial decay" (virtually no ↔ lack).
Đoạn 5: "contaminate freshwater wells used for irrigation" (used for irrigation ↔ needed for crops).
Đoạn 6: "juvenile sea bass and other commercial fish" (juvenile ↔ young).
